overview: Protoceratops andrewsi was a small sheep-sized ceratopsian (~1.8 m) from the Campanian of Mongolia (~75 Ma), known from hundreds of specimens including eggs, embryos and every growth stage — the most complete growth series of any non-avian dinosaur outside Psittacosaurus. Roy Chapman Andrews' 1923 American Museum expeditions found the first dinosaur eggs ever confirmed as such alongside Protoceratops nests.

A famous specimen preserves Protoceratops and Velociraptor locked together in combat — the "Fighting Dinosaurs" — killed and buried simultaneously during a sandstorm or collapsing dune. Protoceratops had a neck frill but no horns — the skull shows the developmental trajectory from small frill in juveniles to large frill in adults, with males likely having larger frills than females.

articles.title: Andrews and the first eggs
articles.body: Roy Chapman Andrews' Central Asiatic Expeditions (1922–1930) found the first confirmed dinosaur eggs at Bayanzag. Initially attributed to a large theropod hypothesised to prey on Protoceratops, the eggs were subsequently identified as Oviraptor eggs — and Oviraptor, previously thought a nest raider, was actually brooding its own eggs. Protoceratops eggs are now known but are smaller and different in shape.

articles.title: Sexual dimorphism and frill
articles.body: Protoceratops shows two skull morphs in adult specimens: one with a taller, more elaborate frill and more robust nasal region; another with a shallower frill. These are tentatively interpreted as male and female, with the larger-frilled morph being male. The frill grew substantially through ontogeny, suggesting it was a socially significant display structure rather than a purely defensive shield.

articles.title: Fighting Dinosaurs
articles.body: The ZPAL MgD-I/95 specimen — preserved in Mongolia since 1971 by Soviet-Mongolian expeditions — shows Velociraptor's hand claw embedded in Protoceratops's neck region while Protoceratops grips Velociraptor's right arm with its beak. Rapid burial by a collapsing sand dune is the most widely accepted explanation for simultaneous preservation of both animals in combat posture. It is one of the most spectacular behavioural snapshots in the entire fossil record.

record.description: Protoceratops andrewsi was a sheep-sized neoceratopsian from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia, known from abundant skulls and skeletons across growth stages.
facts: The famous fighting specimen preserves direct interaction with Velociraptor.
Eggs historically assigned to Protoceratops were oviraptorosaur eggs; some genuine protoceratopsian nesting evidence is now known separately.
Large samples document growth, but strong sexual dimorphism in frill shape has not been demonstrated securely.

presentation.heroLead: A sheep-sized frilled dinosaur from the Gobi Desert, known from so many skeletons at every age that it is a standard reference for how a dinosaur grew.

animalParagraphs: Protoceratops was a stocky, four-legged plant-eater about the size of a sheep, with a parrot-like beak, a broad bony frill at the back of the skull and no true horns. It lived in the sand-dune and oasis landscapes recorded by the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia and equivalent rocks in Inner Mongolia during the Campanian.

Adults reached roughly two metres in length, and hundreds of specimens from hatchlings to old individuals let palaeontologists trace how the frill and nasal boss enlarged with age. Whether the differences seen among adult frills reflect males and females has been tested statistically and not confirmed.

Protoceratops is also famous for what happened around it. The Fighting Dinosaurs specimen preserves one locked in combat with a Velociraptor, and a nest of fifteen juveniles shows that young animals stayed together after hatching. The eggs once attributed to it, however, turned out to belong to the oviraptorosaur Oviraptor.
animalHighlights: A short, deep skull with a hooked beak, cheek teeth in shearing batteries and a frill that grew larger with age.
Hundreds of individuals across all growth stages, one of the best growth series for any dinosaur.
Direct associations with a predator and with a clutch of juveniles are preserved in the fossil record.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: A strong beak and shearing tooth batteries fit tough, low-growing vegetation; the particular plants are not preserved.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Complete articulated skeletons and limb proportions show a four-legged walker; a hand print has also been referred to the genus.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Many complete adult skeletons give reliable lengths; mass estimates of roughly 80 kilograms still depend on the reconstruction method.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Bone proportions are secure; possible skin impressions have been reported, but colour and any tail bristles remain speculative.

locality.name: Bayn Dzak (Flaming Cliffs)
locality.note: Djadokhta Formation. Discovered by the Central Asiatic Expeditions in 1922; the second species P. hellenikorhinus comes from Bayan Mandahu in Inner Mongolia, China.

presentation.classificationSummary: Protoceratops is the name-bearing genus of Protoceratopsidae, a group of small hornless neoceratopsians from Late Cretaceous Asia. It lies outside Ceratopsidae, the horned dinosaurs of North America, but shares with them the frill and cheek-tooth batteries. Two species are recognised: P. andrewsi from Mongolia and P. hellenikorhinus from China.

related.reason: Its predator, preserved locked together with a Protoceratops in the Fighting Dinosaurs specimen.
A smaller protoceratopsid from the same region and a common point of comparison.
An earlier, bipedal ceratopsian that shows what preceded the frilled body plan.

questions.title: Were the frill differences male and female?
questions.copy: A 2015 shape analysis of dozens of skulls found continuous variation rather than two clusters, so sexual dimorphism in the frill is not demonstrated.

questions.title: What was the frill for?
questions.copy: Display, muscle attachment and species recognition have all been proposed. Its late growth is consistent with a signalling role but does not prove it.

questions.title: How did the Fighting Dinosaurs die?
questions.copy: Sudden burial by a collapsing dune or sand flow is the usual explanation for the pair being preserved mid-struggle, but the exact event is inferred, not recorded.

review.ageReviewNote: The core P. andrewsi record is Campanian Djadokhta Formation; P. hellenikorhinus is a separate species from Bayan Mandahu.

specimens.note: A partial skull collected at Bayn Dzak in 1922 and named by Granger and Gregory in 1923; the first of hundreds of specimens recovered from the Djadokhta Formation.

specimens.name: Mounted skeleton
specimens.note: A nearly complete articulated adult skeleton from Bayn Dzak, mounted in New York and one of the specimens underpinning Brown and Schlaikjer's 1940 growth study.

panel.headline: Hundreds of skulls and skeletons from hatchling to adult.
panel.standfirst: Protoceratops andrewsi is one of the most abundantly preserved dinosaurs anywhere. Articulated skeletons, complete skulls, juveniles in nests and even a specimen locked with a predator have come from the Djadokhta Formation since 1922.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every region of the skeleton is represented by many individuals, including complete articulated skeletons and a full growth series from hatchlings to large adults.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls with beaks and tooth batteries, full vertebral columns, girdles, all four limbs with hands and feet, articulated adults, a nest of fifteen juveniles, and a pair of skeletons preserved in combat.
knownRemains.note: The abundance supports detailed anatomy and growth work; it does not by itself settle questions about sexual dimorphism, social behaviour or how the second species relates to the first.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete skulls at every growth stage, with beak, frill, nasal boss and tooth batteries; braincases and endocasts have been studied.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series in articulated skeletons, including the tall-spined tail.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete shoulder and hip girdles, forelimbs and hindlimbs with hands and feet from numerous individuals.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Articulated predator–prey pair, a nest of juveniles, and reported skin impressions; no colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: AMNH 6251 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull found at the Flaming Cliffs in 1922 by the Central Asiatic Expeditions and named by Granger and Gregory the following year. Far more complete skulls followed from the same beds.
specimenCards.meta: Bayn Dzak, Mongolia · Djadokhta Formation · American Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: MPC-D 100/512 · Fighting Dinosaurs
specimenCards.description: Found in 1971 at Tugrikin Shireh by a Polish–Mongolian expedition, this Protoceratops is preserved gripping the arm of a Velociraptor whose foot claw lies against its throat, a rare direct record of predator and prey.
specimenCards.meta: Tugrikin Shireh, Mongolia · Djadokhta Formation · Mongolian Academy of Sciences

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Complete skulls and skeletons across all ages, a clutch of juveniles, a predator–prey pair and the bones of two species from Mongolia and China.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A quadrupedal herbivore whose frill enlarged late in growth, probably for display; juveniles remained together after hatching; the eggs once assigned to it belong to oviraptorosaurs.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether adults can be sexed from the skull, how the two species relate, the extent of any bristles or skin ornament, colour, and details of social behaviour.
